subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: Viral pathogenesis describes how viruses enter, replicate, spread, and cause disease. Understanding each step helps clinicians predict presentation, choose diagnostics, and target therapy.

sections.p: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that rely on host cells for replication. Pathogenesis is shaped by viral tropism, host immunity, and viral evasion strategies.
b: Entry → uncoating → replication → assembly → release
Host factors (receptors, immunity) determine disease severity

sections.p: Viruses vary in genome type (DNA, RNA, retrovirus) and envelope status, influencing stability, transmission, and drug targets.
b: Enveloped viruses (e.g., influenza) are sensitive to detergents
Non‑enveloped viruses (e.g., adenovirus) resist lipid solvents

sections.p: Transmission routes (respiratory, fecal‑oral, blood, vector) dictate initial site of infection and subsequent spread.
b: Respiratory droplets → upper airway epithelium
Bloodborne → hepatocytes (HBV), CD4+ T cells (HIV)
Vector (mosquito) → skin → systemic spread

t.b: Is the virus present? Positive result confirms infection; negative does not exclude early infection.
Has the patient mounted an immune response? IgM = recent infection; IgG = past exposure or immunity.

sections.p: Clinical disease results from direct cytopathic effect, immune‑mediated injury, or chronic persistence.
b: Acute: influenza – fever, cough, myalgia
Chronic: hepatitis B – liver inflammation, cirrhosis risk
Persistent: HIV – CD4 loss, opportunistic infections

sections.p: Combine clinical pattern with targeted laboratory tests; consider local prevalence of tropical infections.
b: Use PCR when rapid, specific identification is needed
Serology useful for timing of infection
Culture rarely needed except for antiviral susceptibility

t.b: Is there leukopenia or lymphocytosis? Lymphopenia may suggest viral infection; normal counts do not rule it out.
Is hepatic injury present? Elevated ALT/AST supports hepatitis viruses; normal values do not exclude early disease.

sections.p: Therapy targets viral replication or modulates host response; prevention relies on vaccines and infection control.
b: Nucleoside analogues (e.g., acyclovir) inhibit viral DNA polymerase – chosen for HSV, VZV
Protease inhibitors block HIV maturation – avoid in severe liver disease
Interferon boosts innate immunity – used for hepatitis C (now replaced by direct‑acting antivirals)
Supportive care: hydration, antipyretics, oxygen

sections.p: Key concepts frequently tested in exams.
b: Order of viral pathogenesis stages
Difference between enveloped vs non‑enveloped virus stability
Mechanism of action of reverse transcriptase inhibitors

whenToSeekHelp: Acute liver failure with hepatitis B
Rapid CD4 decline in HIV infection

faq.q: Why do some viruses cause only mild illness?
faq.a: Limited tropism or effective host immunity restricts damage.

faq.q: What is the role of interferon in viral infections?
faq.a: It induces antiviral proteins that inhibit viral replication.

faq.q: When is a viral PCR preferred over serology?
faq.a: In early infection when antibodies have not yet formed.

exam: List the five stages of viral pathogenesis in order.
Explain why enveloped viruses are more susceptible to disinfectants.
Describe how reverse transcriptase inhibitors interfere with HIV replication.
